**Diagnosis**: The attack succeeded on every tested laboratory image but on 84.8 percent of frames in the moving-vehicle field test. Each number is evidence only for its own capture conditions, and the gap between them does not isolate any one factor, such as distance, viewing angle, lighting, or motion.

**Systems lesson**: A physical attack must be evaluated through the full sensor loop, not on saved benchmark images. The evaluation should optimize the attack over the expected range of transformations (expectation over transformation) and then test it with real captures, and any claimed mitigation, such as spatio-temporal validation or sensor fusion, must be tested against attacks on the complete perception stack.

:::

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The road-sign sticker attack is established as a security threat in @sec-security-privacy-case-study-traffic-sign-attack-6e93.
:::

Physical perturbations also need not be subtle to matter. The perturbations in @fig-graffiti range from a poster covering the whole sign to graffiti-style markings and sticker patches that pass for ordinary vandalism. The associated study evaluates whether these physical modifications induce misclassification through the camera pipeline without digital access to the captured input [@eykholt2018robust].

::: {#fig-graffiti fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Physically Realizable Road-Sign Perturbations**: Physically realizable modifications can cause machine learning models to make incorrect predictions. The three panels show perturbations from the original study, from a subtle full-sign poster to conspicuous graffiti-style camouflage and black-and-white sticker patches that look like ordinary vandalism yet trigger misclassification [@eykholt2018robust]." fig-alt="Photographs of stop signs with conspicuous vandalism-style markings applied, illustrating physical adversarial perturbation as a category."}

![](./images/png/graffiti.png)

:::

The attacker's access determines the evaluation a defense must survive. @Tbl-attack_types distinguishes gradient access, optimization, surrogate transfer, and physical sensor manipulation so that a result under one attack mechanism does not become a claim about all of them.

| **Category**     | **Method**      | **Mechanism**                                                           |
|:-----------------|:----------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Gradient**     | FGSM            | Perturbs inputs along the loss gradient                                 |
|                  | PGD             | Iterative multi-step FGSM refinement                                    |
|                  | JSMA            | Targets the most influential features                                   |
| **Optimization** | C&W             | Minimizes perturbation size subject to misclassification                |
|                  | DeepFool        | Estimates a small boundary-crossing perturbation by local linearization |
|                  | EAD             | Elastic net regularization for sparse perturbations                     |
| **Transfer**     | Transferability | Adversarial examples transfer across models (black-box)                 |
| **Physical**     | Patches         | Printed patches fool detectors in the real world                        |
|                  | 3D Objects      | Sculpted objects deceive sensors in deployment                          |

: **Adversarial Attack Categories**: Attack mechanisms determine defense selection: gradient and optimization attacks require robustness against explicit decision-boundary crossing, transfer attacks test black-box exposure, and physical attacks require evaluation through the deployed sensor loop. {#tbl-attack_types tbl-colwidths="[15,18,67]"}

Medical-imaging attacks can cause misdiagnosis [@tsai2023], while fraud and trading models face analogous manipulation risks. The common vulnerability is reliance on features that remain predictive on clean data but fail under crafted perturbations [@goodfellow2015explaining; @madry2018towards]. Defense shifts the resource cost: adversarial training adds training work [@bai2021], while runtime detection such as feature squeezing adds inference evaluations [@xu2018]. The choice among these spending points motivates the defenses in @sec-robust-ai-input-attack-detection-defense-19d3.

\Needspace{14\baselineskip}

### Data poisoning {#sec-robust-ai-data-poisoning-4b55}

The attacks so far perturb a fixed model at inference time. Poisoning instead changes the data from which the model learns. Systems that accept user contributions must distinguish evidence for learning from instructions that merely request a response. Microsoft's Tay incident illustrates the broader danger of adversarial interaction: the company reported a coordinated attack that defeated its filtering and stress testing within a day of launch [@microsoft2016tay]. The public account does not detail the mechanism, but the robustness lesson does not depend on it. Once live interaction can shape a model's later behavior, every user is a potential contributor of training evidence, and coordinated users can supply it on purpose. For systems that do learn from user feedback\index{Data Poisoning!online feedback manipulation}, the engineering question is therefore which contributions may enter training and how their influence can be audited.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Data poisoning, the corruption of training data or updates so that the learned model misbehaves later, and its sequence of admission, training, and exploitation are established in @sec-security-privacy-data-poisoning-351f.
:::

Automated collection, web scraping, and crowdsourced annotation make poisoning a pipeline-integrity problem: the system must identify compromised contributions before the learner incorporates them.

A classic early formulation in ML security is the attack by @biggio2012poisoning on support-vector machines\index{Data Poisoning!support-vector machines}. More recent poisoning work broadens the target to web-scale and generative-model data pipelines [see also @shan2024]. The dirty-label attack sampled in @fig-dirty-label-example corrupts training data by pairing cat images with misleading 'dog' captions, attempting to induce fraudulent associations during multimodal pretraining. The consequences are especially severe in high-stakes domains like healthcare, where even small disruptions to training data can lead to dangerous misdiagnoses [@marulli2022].

::: {#fig-dirty-label-example fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Dirty-Label Data Poisoning**: Mismatched image-text pairs represent a dirty-label poisoning attack where cat images are paired with misleading 'dog' captions in training data. Incorporating these corrupted pairs can cause models to learn incorrect multimodal associations." fig-alt="Three panels labeled 'Dirty-label poison data', each showing a cat image paired with a misleading text caption that calls the image a dog: 'A dog on the grass', 'Animal art dog pencil drawings', and 'Dog digital art...'."}

![](./images/png/dirty_label_example.png)

:::

Because admitting a poisoned record does not by itself guarantee that training will learn the attacker's behavior, the evidence that matters is behavioral, and it differs across the four objective classes of the security threat model: availability, targeted, backdoor\index{Backdoor Attack!trigger pattern}, and subpopulation\index{Subpopulation Poisoning!fairness impact} poisoning. The robustness question is which evidence exposes each class and what that evidence costs [@oprea2022]. Successful availability attacks\index{Data Poisoning!availability attack} can lower aggregate validation accuracy, giving broad evaluation a signal to investigate. Targeted\index{Data Poisoning!targeted class compromise} and subpopulation attacks can leave that aggregate nearly intact, making evaluation on the named targets and cohorts particularly important. Backdoors can also preserve clean-data accuracy while responding to a trigger the evaluator has never seen, as the BadNets pixel-pattern trigger does [@gu2017badnets]; possible detection strategies include trigger search, canary inputs, and activation-space inspection when poisoned and clean representations separate [@tran2018spectral].

::: {#lhs-robust-ai-archetype-b-dlrm-at-scale-fake-profile-injection .callout-lighthouse title="Archetype B (DLRM at Scale): Fake profile injection"}

Archetype B (DLRM at Scale) is especially exposed to **fake profile injection**\index{Fake Profile Injection!definition}. Because recommendation systems often use online learning to adapt to user trends in real time, an adversary can create a network of "sybil" accounts\index{Fake Profile Injection!sybil network}, fake identities controlled by the same attacker, that interact with specific items to artificially boost their popularity or associate them with high-value demographics. This poisoning bypasses traditional firewalls because the malicious interactions look like legitimate user behavior, motivating checks on contributor identity, interaction patterns, and learned representations. Spectral-signature defenses\index{Spectral Signature} (developed in @sec-robust-ai-sanitization-preprocessing-f883) search activation patterns for suspicious separation, but their effectiveness depends on whether the poisoned and clean contributions separate in that representation.

:::

Poisoned records can resemble legitimate data, so clean aggregate validation accuracy alone cannot establish that a training corpus is trustworthy. Detectability depends on the attacker's objective and on which records, representations, and behavioral slices the evaluator inspects. Attacks may originate from internal actors with privileged pipeline access or from external adversaries who exploit weak points in data collection, particularly in crowdsourced environments or open data pipelines that lack integrity checks and lineage tracking.

::: {#exmp-robust-ai-targeted-poisoning-classification .callout-example title="Targeted poisoning classification"}

**Scenario**: An attacker modifies the labels of a small subset of training data so that one deployed classifier consistently maps a particular protected class or object pattern to the wrong output.

**Diagnosis**: This is a targeted attack\index{Targeted Attack}. The attacker is not trying to degrade overall model performance; they are inducing a specific error while preserving enough general accuracy that aggregate validation metrics may still look healthy.

**Systems lesson**: Defending against targeted poisoning requires slice-level evaluation, provenance checks, and canary examples for high-risk classes. Aggregate accuracy alone is a weak detector because the attack is designed to hide inside otherwise normal performance.

:::

Distributed and federated training adds a contributor axis to the same threat. A malicious client need not insert a visible record into a central corpus; it can submit a model update chosen to move the aggregate, implant a backdoor, or exploit sybil identities to gain disproportionate weight. Archetype C (Federated MobileNet) makes this concrete: the server aggregates updates from a large population of smartphone-class clients whose raw data it never sees. Contributor-level checks can screen updates before aggregation, while held-out behavioral tests can reveal harmful effects in the resulting global model. The evaluation must vary the number and coordination of malicious contributors, their data heterogeneity, participation schedule, and knowledge of the aggregation rule. Global clean accuracy is again insufficient: the gate needs attack success on the trigger or target subpopulation, contributor-level anomaly recall, and the clean-utility cost of robust aggregation. Krum, coordinate-wise median, and trimmed mean tolerate bounded Byzantine behavior only under their stated assumptions [@blanchard2017machine; @yin2018byzantine]; high dimensionality and non-i.i.d. client updates can make honest contributors look anomalous. These rules also change the collective. A mean can be computed by an AllReduce that sums partial results, but a median, trimmed mean, or Krum selection needs the individual updates, and a direct gather-based implementation raises per-worker traffic by about a factor of $\DataParallelDegree/2$ relative to ring AllReduce, where $\DataParallelDegree$ here counts the contributing replicas rather than accelerators. That cost lands on $\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)$ in the Fleet Law unless it overlaps with computation. Provenance, participation limits, robust aggregation, and held-out canaries must therefore work together rather than treating one distance rule as a poisoning proof.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The traffic cost of gather-based robust aggregation relative to ring AllReduce is established in @sec-security-privacy-gradient-sync-integrity.
:::

#### Data poisoning attack methods {#sec-robust-ai-data-poisoning-attack-methods-d168}

The four categories above describe an attacker's *objective*; the attack *mechanism* depends on the attacker's access to the system and knowledge of the data pipeline. As diagrammed in @fig-poisoning-impact, all of them share a common shape: a poisoned record enters the training pipeline alongside clean data and attempts to alter the resulting model's behavior. The most direct mechanism is label modification, where an attacker selects a subset of training samples and alters their labels, flipping $\ExampleLabel= 1$ to $\ExampleLabel= 0$ or reassigning categories in multi-class settings. Even small-scale label corruption can shift decision boundaries significantly.

::: {#fig-poisoning-impact fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Data Poisoning Impact**: A nominal pipeline (top) and a poisoned pipeline (bottom) pass through the same four stages. In the illustrated successful attack, a poisoned record admitted at ingestion contaminates the training corpus, pulls the optimizer's gradients toward the attacker's trigger, and yields a backdoored model whose clean accuracy can remain intact, so aggregate validation alone can miss it." fig-alt="Two rows of four panels under the headings ingestion, training corpus, optimization, and trained model, joined by arrows. In the nominal row, three green clean records arrive, the corpus is a grid of green record tiles, a gray step descends into the minimum of a set of loss contours, and a straight decision boundary separates hollow and filled points. In the poisoned row, the middle arriving record is red, one tile of the corpus grid is red, a red step bends away from the contour minimum toward a red trigger diamond while a dashed gray path shows the clean direction, and the same decision boundary now has a small red dashed pocket around a trigger diamond on the filled side, labeled backdoor pocket and clean accuracy intact. The arrows in the poisoned row are red."}
![](images/svg/poisoning-impact.svg)
:::

After label modification, the attacker can keep the label intact and corrupt the features instead, the strategy known as **clean-label poisoning**\index{Clean-Label Poisoning!definition}. Because every label is correct, label audits cannot flag these records. Imperceptible image perturbations, subtle shifts in structured fields, and fixed trigger patterns all aim for the same outcome: the training example still appears legitimate, but it bends the learned decision boundary toward a future failure. Generative methods and data-synthesis tools raise the same risk at larger scale because they can create natural-looking examples whose only purpose is to distort what the model learns.

Whether those examples become poisoning depends on the data boundary. Web scraping, social media feeds, crowdsourced annotation, and untrusted user submissions all allow poisoned records to enter upstream and pass through weak cleaning checks in a "trusted" form. Physical systems add a second path: a sticker on a road sign is an inference-time adversarial attack when the car sees it, but harvesting that image into a training corpus creates a potential poisoning path only if the contribution serves an attack on the learner. Correctly labeled examples of such inputs can instead help train resistance to them. Online learning systems tighten the feedback loop further, allowing an attacker to introduce small increments of malicious data until model behavior drifts without a single obvious anomaly. @Fig-poisoning-attack-example draws the collaborative form of the same boundary, the contributor axis already described for federated training, in which one malicious client's update reaches every participant through aggregation.

::: {#fig-poisoning-attack-example fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Collaborative Poisoning via Aggregation**: In a collaborative learning setting, multiple clients each train on local data and contribute model updates to a central server that aggregates them into a shared global model. A single malicious participant can inject poisoned updates that the server folds into the aggregated model, so the corruption spreads to every client without any one obvious anomaly. This attack surface differs from adversarial examples because it targets the model during *training* rather than at *inference*." fig-alt="A violet aggregation server box at the top shows the weighted mean w t plus 1 equals w t plus the sum over k of n k over n times delta w k, and an inset plot of update vectors drawn from the point w t: three amber honest updates point steeply upward in a narrow fan, one red update delta w 2 points nearly sideways, and a thicker violet aggregate arrow sits between them, tilted away from the honest fan. A row of clients sits below: client 1, a red malicious client 2, client 3, an ellipsis, and client N, each holding a row of small green data tiles, with two red tiles in client 2. Each benign client sends an amber update arrow, delta w 1, delta w 3, and delta w N, up to the server, while client 2 sends a red update delta w 2 marked poisoned. Dashed red arrows labeled w t plus 1 run from the server down to each client."}
![](images/svg/poisoning-attack.svg)
:::

Insiders such as annotators or data vendors can exploit knowledge of the model and training procedure to make these attacks harder to detect. Clean benchmark performance therefore does not establish training-data integrity.

#### Art protection via poisoning case study {#sec-robust-ai-case-study-art-protection-via-poisoning-6106}

Data poisoning is not always malicious. Researchers have begun exploring it as a defensive tool, particularly for protecting creative work from unauthorized use by generative AI models.

Nightshade, developed by researchers at the University of Chicago, aims to deter unauthorized training by poisoning images that a scraper may collect [@shan2024]. It does not block scraping itself. Its perturbations preserve the apparent image content while changing how a model learns from it; the reported experiments show targeted concept corruption when the modified images enter the tested training pipelines.

The dose-response matrix in @fig-poisoning charts this progressive corruption across four poison doses (0 to 300 samples) and eight prompt concepts: as the dose increases, Stable Diffusion XL outputs morph away from source concepts (generating cows for "car" or cats for "dog") under the tested training conditions. These outputs demonstrate changed behavior without, by themselves, identifying the internal representation that caused it. The experiment demonstrates concept poisoning\index{Data Poisoning!concept poisoning}: poisoned samples distort a model's semantic associations.

::: {#fig-poisoning fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Concept Poisoning Dose-Response**: Stable Diffusion XL outputs across four poison doses (clean, 50, 100, 300 samples) and eight source prompts (dog, car, handbag, hat, fantasy art, cubism, cartoon, concept art). As the dose grows, outputs morph from the intended source concept toward the attacker's destination concept, demonstrating Nightshade-style concept poisoning of a pretrained model." fig-alt="4x8 grid of Stable Diffusion XL outputs. Rows are poison doses (clean, 50, 100, 300); columns are source prompts (Dog, Car, Handbag, Hat, Fantasy art, Cubism, Cartoon, Concept Art). Outputs morph toward destination concepts as dose grows."}

![](./images/png/poisoning_example.png)

:::

The Nightshade experiments also report effects on concepts related to the poisoned target. This spillover extends the observed attack beyond the exact target prompt, but its reach depends on the model, poison construction, and training procedure. The same technique used to protect artistic content could also be repurposed to sabotage legitimate training pipelines, highlighting the dual-use dilemma[^fn-dual-use-ml] at the heart of machine learning security.

[^fn-dual-use-ml]: **Dual-Use Dilemma**\index{Dual-Use Dilemma!ML security}: The structural tension that defensive ML capabilities (adversarial training, data poisoning tools, red-teaming frameworks) are simultaneously offensive capabilities. This creates an arms race where defensive research publications become attack playbooks. For ML systems engineering, the consequence is architectural: robustness mechanisms must assume attacker knowledge of the defense, ruling out security-through-obscurity and motivating formal guarantees where feasible and adaptive empirical evaluation within the remaining threat model.

The mechanics of these input-level attacks, from adversarial perturbations and data poisoning to their interaction with natural distribution shifts (@sec-robust-ai-environmental-shifts-a2cf), define the threat surface. The next question is *how* to engineer the algorithmic defenses required to protect production models against them.

## Adversarial Defenses {#sec-robust-ai-input-attack-detection-defense-19d3}

The classifier that called a panda a gibbon in @fig-adversarial-googlenet was not broken by random noise; a perturbation budget of 0.007 per pixel, spent along the gradient sign, was enough. Defending a deployed perception model against that attacker requires a threat model that names the attacker's access and a budget for testing and mitigation. The resulting robustness claim must state what the system pays in clean accuracy, training compute, inference latency, or operational coverage.

### Adversarial defense workflow {#sec-robust-ai-adversarial-attack-defenses-1dc8}

The adversarial-defense workflow\index{Adversarial Defense!four-layer workflow} has four ordered layers:

1. **Define the threat model**: Specify the perturbation budget, attacker knowledge, and whether the attack occurs at inference time or during training.
2. **Choose the robustness budget**: Decide whether to spend the budget in training, certification, input detection, or serving-time guardrails.
3. **Measure the trade-off**: Evaluate both sides of the defense, because improving worst-case behavior can reduce clean accuracy, raise inference latency, or multiply training cost.
4. **Keep evaluation adversarial**: Test the defense against attacks stronger than the ones used to design it.

The order matters because an uncalibrated threat model makes the budget and evaluation loop meaningless.

For model-facing perturbation threats, the most direct training-time defense is **adversarial training**\index{Adversarial Training!definition}, which incorporates adversarial examples into the training process itself. The mechanism reuses the attacks of the previous section as a data generator. Each training step augments the batch\index{Adversarial Training!PGD batch augmentation} with perturbed copies of its own inputs, so the model is trained on the high-loss points an attacker would choose. @Lst-adversarial-training implements this pattern using FGSM to generate perturbations and mix clean and adversarial examples in each batch.

::: {#lst-adversarial-training lst-cap="**Adversarial Training Pseudocode**: Framework-neutral adversarial training using FGSM-style perturbations during training, mixing clean and perturbed data to improve robustness against gradient-based attacks."}

```{.text}
function adversarial_training_step(model, clean_batch, labels, epsilon):
    logits = model(clean_batch)
    clean_loss = loss(logits, labels)

    input_gradient = gradient(clean_loss, clean_batch)
    perturbation = epsilon * sign(input_gradient)
    adversarial_batch = stop_gradient(
        clip(clean_batch + perturbation, valid_input_range))

    mixed_batch = concatenate(clean_batch, adversarial_batch)
    mixed_labels = concatenate(labels, labels)

    return loss(model(mixed_batch), mixed_labels)
```

:::

In @lst-adversarial-training, the sign step bounds each coordinate's change by the perturbation budget, while clipping keeps the perturbed input inside the valid input range (for example, $[0,1]$ for normalized pixels). Concatenation doubles the effective batch size. The stop-gradient operation treats generated adversarial inputs as fixed during the outer weight update, rather than differentiating through attack construction. The caller differentiates the returned loss with respect to the model parameters and performs the optimizer update. The perturbation budget $\AdversarialPerturbationBudget$ (the `epsilon` argument) bounds the allowed input change, while the attack algorithm determines how effectively it searches that set; computation reuse can reduce its training overhead [@shafahi2019adversarial].

Adversarial example generation increases training time because each training step requires additional forward and backward passes through the model [@madry2018towards; @bai2021]. Memory overhead depends on whether the implementation stores clean and adversarial examples together, recomputes perturbations, or reuses gradient information. Iterative attacks like PGD add multiple optimization steps, so the implementation must budget that gradient work; optimized variants reduce overhead by reusing computations\index{Adversarial Training!free gradient reuse} rather than treating every attack step as a separate full training pass [@shafahi2019adversarial].

A robustness recipe that increases model capacity also adds memory and training cost. The perturbation budget and training recipe require matched clean and adversarial validation, and the perspective below shows why that matching decides what the robustness tax actually is.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: robustness-tax-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE ROBUSTNESS TAX (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-robust-ai-adversarial-attack-defenses-1dc8
# │
# │ Goal: Expose an invalid clean-versus-attacked accuracy subtraction.
# │ Show: A 26-point cross-condition gap that is not a clean-accuracy tax.
# │ How: Standard ResNet-50 clean accuracy from Literature.Series.ImageNetTestbedShift
# │      (76.1%) against an assumed robust-model attacked accuracy (~50%).
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt

# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
class RobustnessTaxAnalysis:
    """Quantify the utility-robustness trade-off."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    from mlsysim import Models

    m = Models.Vision.ResNet50
    from mlsysim import Literature

    standard_clean_acc = next(r["val"] for r in Literature.Series.ImageNetTestbedShift.entries if r["model"] == "resnet50")
    robust_model_attacked_acc = 50.0  # scenario assumption: an adversarially trained ImageNet model at 4/255

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    cross_condition_gap = standard_clean_acc - robust_model_attacked_acc

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    from mlsysim.fmt import check

    check(75.5 <= standard_clean_acc <= 76.5, "Prose quotes 76 percent for the standard ResNet-50.")
    check(cross_condition_gap > 20, "Illustrative cross-condition gap should exceed 20 points")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_percent, fmt_pp

    clean_acc_str = fmt_percent(round(standard_clean_acc) / 100, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    robust_acc_str = fmt_percent(robust_model_attacked_acc / 100, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    cross_condition_gap_pp_str = fmt_pp(round(cross_condition_gap), precision=0, commas=False)
```

::: {#psp-robust-ai-robustness-tax .callout-perspective title="Pricing the robustness tax correctly"}

Suppose a standard ResNet-50\index{ResNet-50} records `{python} RobustnessTaxAnalysis.clean_acc_str` Top-1 accuracy on clean ImageNet, while an adversarially trained model records about `{python} RobustnessTaxAnalysis.robust_acc_str` under a specified $\ell_\infty$ attack at $\AdversarialPerturbationBudget=4/255$, the budget conventionally used for ImageNet. Subtracting these values yields `{python} RobustnessTaxAnalysis.cross_condition_gap_pp_str`, but that gap compares different models under different evaluation conditions. It is not the clean-accuracy cost of robustness.

The clean-accuracy tax\index{Robustness Tax!clean-accuracy trade-off} must compare standard and robust models on the same clean test set. The robustness benefit must compare those models under the same attack, perturbation budget, and attack strength. The four cells are the standard model on clean data, the standard model under attack, the robust model on clean data, and the robust model under attack. The tax is the first minus the third, the benefit is the fourth minus the second, and the quoted pair supplies only the first and the fourth. Reporting all four cells prevents an apparent trade-off from mixing a model effect with an evaluation-condition effect.

**Systems insight**: Robustness can reduce clean accuracy and increase compute, but each tax needs a like-for-like baseline. A deployment gate should report clean accuracy, empirical robust accuracy, attack specification, and evaluation cost separately.

:::

The robustness compute penalty (principle \ref{pri-robustness-compute-penalty}) quantifies this cost: PGD-style adversarial robustness can demand several times more compute per epoch than standard optimization because each batch runs inner attack steps. In Fleet Law terms (@eq-fleet-law) the multiplier lands on $\IronLawComputeTime$. At a fixed worker count it adds local work, but the elapsed-time penalty depends on reuse and on which term limits the step. Adding workers changes communication and synchronization costs with $\DeviceCount$ and may not recover the original duration. Notebook \ref{nbk-robust-ai-cost-defense} makes the multiplier concrete.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: adversarial-payback-notebook
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ADVERSARIAL ATTACK PAYBACK (NOTEBOOK)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: "The Cost of Defense" .callout-notebook
# │
# │ Goal: Quantify the compute overhead of adversarial training.
# │ Show: training_slowdown ≈ 8x—inline in notebook result.
# │ How: total time = standard time + PGD steps × standard time.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_count, fmt_multiple

class AdversarialPayback:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ──────────────────────────────────────────
    std_passes = 1
    n_pgd_steps = 7  # Illustrative PGD-7 adversarial-training scenario
    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ───────────────────────────────────────
    # Each training step requires generating an attack (7 forward/backward passes)
    # total steps per batch = 1 (std) + 7 (attack) = 8
    slowdown = std_passes + n_pgd_steps
    # ┌── 3. GUARD ─────────────────────────────────────────
    check(slowdown == 8, f"Slowdown {slowdown} unexpected")
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ────────────────────────────────────────
    ap_std_passes_str = fmt(std_passes, precision=0, commas=False)
    ap_n_pgd_steps_str = fmt(n_pgd_steps, precision=0, commas=False)
    ap_total_passes_str = fmt_count(slowdown, precision=0, commas=False)
    ap_slowdown_mult_str = fmt_multiple(slowdown, precision=0, commas=False)
```

::: {#nbk-robust-ai-cost-defense .callout-notebook title="The cost of defense"}

**Problem**: A team is training a robust classifier for an autonomous vehicle. Instead of the single FGSM step in @lst-adversarial-training, it uses adversarial training\index{Adversarial Training!accuracy cost} with a seven-step PGD attack (PGD-7)\index{Projected Gradient Descent Attack!multi-step training overhead} that searches for a high-loss perturbation inside a specified norm ball for every training batch, and, following the standard PGD adversarial-training recipe [@madry2018towards], it trains on the adversarial batch alone rather than on the listing's doubled clean-plus-adversarial batch. How much does this extra attack-generation work slow down the training run?

**Math**:
In this example, generating the adversarial input uses $\AttackStepsPgd$ additional gradient steps per training sample, each a forward and backward pass with respect to the input, before the one weight-update pass on the adversarial batch. The estimate treats each attack step as equal in cost to the standard training pass, with no reuse; it is a work model rather than a measured wall-clock slowdown. By the same accounting, the FGSM listing spends one attack pass plus an update pass over a batch twice the original size, about three standard passes in all, so PGD-7 trades a further factor of more than two in training work for a stronger inner attack.

1. **Forward/backward passes**: `{python} AdversarialPayback.ap_std_passes_str` (Standard) + `{python} AdversarialPayback.ap_n_pgd_steps_str` (Attack Generation) = `{python} AdversarialPayback.ap_total_passes_str` total passes.
2. **Training slowdown**\index{Training!slowdown}: `{python} AdversarialPayback.ap_slowdown_mult_str` under the equal-cost-pass assumption.
3. **Utility evidence**: The added work must be justified by measured robust accuracy under the specified attack. Generalization to other attacks requires separate evaluation. Pricing any clean-accuracy cost requires the like-for-like comparison in perspective \ref{psp-robust-ai-robustness-tax}, not a subtraction of robust accuracy from another model's clean accuracy.

**Systems insight**: In this PGD-7 work model, the team budgets `{python} AdversarialPayback.ap_slowdown_mult_str` the baseline compute before measuring the robustness benefit or actual elapsed-time penalty. In a machine learning fleet, robustness is not a setting that can be switched on; it is a budget the team spends, and the budget must be justified by the failure consequence of the component being hardened.

:::

For lower-risk components, external guardrails such as input filtering and output verification can cost less than training intrinsic robustness into the weights, provided adaptive evaluation (@sec-robust-ai-evaluation-testing-4b54) supports acceptable residual risk against an attacker who knows the guardrail. Passing a finite set of attacks does not prove that no bypass exists. Safety-critical paths more often justify the training and certification budget.

::: {#exmp-robust-ai-defense-selection .callout-example title="Defense selection by threat model"}

**Scenario**: Production teams must select defenses across three distinct system settings: an image classifier facing evasion attacks, a recommendation system facing training data poisoning, and a fraud detector facing natural distribution shift.

**Diagnosis**: An inference-time input filter alone cannot meet all three needs. It adds work on the image classifier's serving path, but does not establish the integrity of recommendation training data or track changes in the fraud detector's deployment population.

**Systems lesson**: Defense selection must be tailored to the threat model. Adversarial training targets the specified evasion threat, source controls, sanitization, and robust training objectives (@sec-robust-ai-data-poisoning-defenses-d070) limit some poisoning mechanisms, and drift monitoring identifies shifts for investigation. Each choice needs evaluation against its own failure conditions; detection alone does not restore valid predictions.

:::

#### Certified defenses {#sec-robust-ai-certified-defenses}

Adversarial training provides empirical resistance that must be tested against the deployment threat model. It can generalize beyond the examples generated during training, but attack evaluation alone does not prove invariance throughout an allowed perturbation set. **Certified robustness**\index{Certified Robustness!definition} offers a mathematical guarantee\index{Certified Robustness!mathematical guarantee}: for a given input $\ModelInput$ and radius $\AdversarialPerturbationBudget$, no perturbation $\|\AdversarialPerturbation\|_\PerturbationNormOrder< \AdversarialPerturbationBudget$ exists that changes the model's prediction. This certifies local prediction stability, not that the unchanged prediction is correct. The certified radius is a provable lower bound on the input-perturbation part of the robustness margin that compression and other efficiency changes must preserve. The guarantee formalizes the intuition, met in the pipeline overview, that a robust model limits how quickly its outputs can change as its inputs change. The model's **Lipschitz constant**\index{Lipschitz Constant!definition}[^fn-lipschitz-continuity-bound] bounds that rate, so a prediction cannot change within any radius over which the largest possible score change stays below its top-class margin. A widely used technique for scaling this idea to high-dimensional inputs like ImageNet is **randomized smoothing**\index{Randomized Smoothing!definition}. Instead of classifying $\ModelInput$ directly, it classifies the smoothed function $\SmoothedClassifier(\ModelInput)$, defined as the most probable class predicted by the base classifier\index{Randomized Smoothing!Gaussian smoothing} $\ModelPredictor$ under Gaussian noise: $\SmoothedClassifier(\ModelInput) = \operatorname{arg\,max}_\ClassIndex \Pr(\ModelPredictor(\ModelInput+\RandomizedSmoothingNoise) = \ClassIndex)$ where $\RandomizedSmoothingNoise \sim \GaussianDistribution(\ZeroVector, \SmoothingNoiseStandardDeviation^2 \IdentityMatrix)$.

[^fn-lipschitz-continuity-bound]: **Lipschitz Continuity**\index{Lipschitz Continuity!robustness}: A mathematical property that bounds how much a function's output changes relative to its input change ($\lVert \ModelPredictor(\ModelInput) - \ModelPredictor(\AlternateModelInput) \rVert \le \LipschitzConstant\lVert \ModelInput- \AlternateModelInput\rVert$). A small Lipschitz constant $(\LipschitzConstant)$ limits score movement, but it does not by itself prevent a label flip. A robustness certificate additionally requires the top-class score margin over the runner-up to exceed the worst-case score change within the perturbation radius; reducing $\LipschitzConstant$ can enlarge that certified radius\index{Lipschitz Constant!certified radius trade-off}, though enforcing a low constant can trade away clean-data accuracy and add training cost.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: randomized-smoothing-radius
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ RANDOMIZED SMOOTHING CERTIFIED RADIUS (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-robust-ai-certified-defenses—binary smoothing example.
# │
# │ Goal:    Compute the binary special-case certified radius.
# │ Show:    p_A=0.999, sigma=0.5 gives R≈1.5.
# │ How:     R = sigma * Phi^{-1}(p_A).
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from statistics import NormalDist
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt

# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
class RandomizedSmoothingRadius:
    """Compute a binary randomized-smoothing radius."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    p_top = 0.999
    sigma = 0.5

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    from statistics import NormalDist

    radius = sigma * NormalDist().inv_cdf(p_top)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    from mlsysim.fmt import check

    check(1.54 < radius < 1.55, f"Unexpected smoothing radius: {radius}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    from mlsysim.fmt import fmt

    rs_p_top_str = fmt(p_top, precision=3, commas=False)
    rs_sigma_str = fmt(sigma, precision=1, commas=False)
    rs_radius_str = fmt(radius, precision=1, commas=False)
```

@cohen2019certified proved a tight multiclass bound\index{Randomized Smoothing!certified radius bound} for the certified radius $\CertifiedRadius$ using a lower bound on the top-class probability $\SmoothedTopClassProbability$ and an upper bound on the runner-up probability $\SmoothedRunnerUpProbability$: $\CertifiedRadius= \frac{\SmoothingNoiseStandardDeviation}{2}\left(\StandardNormalCumulativeDistribution^{-1}(\SmoothedTopClassProbability) - \StandardNormalCumulativeDistribution^{-1}(\SmoothedRunnerUpProbability)\right)$, where $\StandardNormalCumulativeDistribution^{-1}$ is the inverse standard normal CDF. In the binary special case, where $\SmoothedRunnerUpProbability= 1 - \SmoothedTopClassProbability$, this reduces to $\CertifiedRadius= \SmoothingNoiseStandardDeviation\StandardNormalCumulativeDistribution^{-1}(\SmoothedTopClassProbability)$. This Gaussian-smoothing bound certifies a Euclidean ($\ell_2$) perturbation radius, measured in the same units as the input to which the noise is added; it does not automatically certify the other norms used in attack benchmarks. If a binary decision has top-class probability $\SmoothedTopClassProbability$ = `{python} RandomizedSmoothingRadius.rs_p_top_str` under noise $\SmoothingNoiseStandardDeviation$ = `{python} RandomizedSmoothingRadius.rs_sigma_str`, the simplified radius is approximately `{python} RandomizedSmoothingRadius.rs_radius_str` in those input units. For an image scaled to $[0,1]$, that radius bounds the Euclidean length of the whole perturbation vector. It is not directly comparable to the per-coordinate $\ell_\infty$ budget of the robustness-tax comparison, because an $\ell_\infty$ perturbation of size $\AdversarialPerturbationBudget$ spread over $\InputCoordinateCount$ pixels can have Euclidean length up to $\AdversarialPerturbationBudget\sqrt{\InputCoordinateCount}$, so a per-pixel budget that looks tiny can correspond to a long Euclidean vector on a high-dimensional image.

The multiclass case rarely estimates the runner-up probability separately. Because the class probabilities sum to one, no competing class can exceed $1 - \SmoothedTopClassProbability$, so a lower bound on $\SmoothedTopClassProbability$ alone also bounds every competitor. Estimating that lower bound from samples turns certification into a statistical estimation problem and adds a confidence level to the certificate; an observed class frequency alone is not a certified probability bound. Certification also carries accuracy and compute trade-offs. On ImageNet, the same work reports nontrivial certified accuracy for randomized smoothing, including certification at radius 0.5, but certification requires sampling many noise vectors per inference to estimate class probabilities with sufficient confidence. The increase in inference latency\index{Randomized Smoothing!inference latency overhead} makes the sample budget a deployment constraint. Two designs keep certification outside the tight serving budget. Asynchronous auditing certifies a sampled fraction of served requests offline, so the fleet learns how often its answers were certifiable without delaying any of them. A selective safety interlock certifies only the requests routed to a safety-critical action, such as a braking decision, and lets the remaining traffic take the uncertified path.

Certified defenses cover one part of the adversarial workflow. Production systems still need detection paths for suspicious inputs, mitigation strategies that change training or serving behavior, and evaluation procedures that verify which threat models remain covered.

#### Detection techniques {#sec-robust-ai-detection-techniques-0e7e}

Detecting adversarial examples before they reach the model forms the first line of defense only when the signal reaches a serving decision: reject, transform, route, or audit. A population-level signal asks whether a window of current inputs still resembles the reference population. The two-sample tests of @sec-robust-ai-statistical-significance-testing-dfde serve here unchanged. A KS test\index{Kolmogorov-Smirnov Test!adversarial detection}, or the Anderson-Darling test\index{Anderson-Darling Test}, a variant that weights differences in the distribution tails more heavily, can flag a traffic window whose inputs no longer resemble the reference. Such an alert does not identify an individual request as adversarial; per-request rejection requires an additional decision rule. These tests also inherit the drift monitors' blind spot, since an adversarial perturbation can preserve each feature's marginal distribution while corrupting the joint structure that joint-distribution or embedding-space comparisons would expose.

An attack that preserves marginal distributions can evade that signal, motivating a complementary comparison under input transformations. **Feature squeezing**\index{Feature Squeezing!definition}[^fn-feature-squeeze-defense] [@xu2018] reduces input-space complexity through color bit-depth reduction or spatial smoothing\index{Feature Squeezing!bit-depth reduction}, then compares the model's prediction before and after the transformation. A large prediction change flags sensitivity to the transformation. It does not by itself establish malicious intent or identify which image detail caused the change; legitimate inputs can also trigger the detector.

[^fn-feature-squeeze-defense]: **Feature Squeezing**\index{Feature Squeezing!adversarial defense}: Defense proposed by @xu2018 that reduces input precision (for example, 256 to 16 color levels) or applies spatial smoothing (median filtering) to disrupt some fine-grained perturbations. Such transformations can also alter useful clean-input features and do not cover every attack mechanism. In their evaluation, feature squeezing eliminated many adversarial examples while maintaining high clean accuracy; adaptive attacks require validation before treating the defense as production-ready.

Another signal asks whether the model is uncertain about its own answer. An uncertainty estimate can route an input for rejection\index{Uncertainty Estimation!Monte Carlo dropout}, human review, or a more robust model. Bayesian neural networks\index{Bayesian Neural Networks!uncertainty estimation} estimate uncertainty by placing a probability distribution over each weight and averaging predictions over sampled weights, so disagreement among those samples signals uncertainty, while ensemble methods\index{Deep Ensemble!uncertainty estimation} compare predictions from independently trained models and use disagreement as the warning signal [@lakshminarayanan2017]. Their detection value depends on whether uncertainty distinguishes harmful inputs from legitimate ones under the chosen attack. Repeated predictions add inference work, so deployments must evaluate both missed attacks and serving cost rather than assume that a more expensive estimator detects more.

Dropout, the training-time regularizer that randomly deactivates neurons [@hinton2012improvingneuralnetworkspreventing], offers a cheaper approximation to that weight sampling. It can be repurposed for uncertainty estimation through **Monte Carlo dropout**\index{Monte Carlo Dropout!definition}[^fn-mc-dropout-inference] at inference time, where multiple forward passes with different dropout masks approximate the uncertainty distribution. Monte Carlo dropout is itself an approximate Bayesian method. Its uncertainty estimates must be validated on the deployment population rather than ranked by the original purpose of dropout. Hybrid approaches that combine dropout with lightweight ensemble methods or Bayesian approximations balance computational efficiency with estimation quality, making uncertainty-based detection more practical for production deployment.

[^fn-mc-dropout-inference]: **Monte Carlo dropout**\index{Monte Carlo Dropout!approximate Bayesian inference}\index{Dropout!MC, inference cost}: Proposed by @gal2016dropout, MC dropout reinterprets dropout as approximate Bayesian inference by keeping dropout active across repeated stochastic forward passes. The variance across predictions provides an uncertainty estimate with no architectural changes. Each additional sample adds inference work, so deployments must select the sample count against their latency and uncertainty budgets.

#### Other defense strategies {#sec-robust-ai-defense-strategies-cb2d}

Adversarial training, certification, and detection do not exhaust the options. The remaining strategies move the spending point rather than eliminating the cost. **Defensive distillation**\index{Defensive Distillation!definition} [@papernot2016] teaches a student model from the teacher's soft labels, but its apparent adversarial protection proved vulnerable to attacks that bypassed the resulting gradient masking [@carlini2017]. It illustrates why making an attack optimizer fail is not evidence that nearby adversarial inputs are absent. Input preprocessing spends the defense budget at serving time: image denoising, JPEG compression, random resizing, padding, and random transformations try to erase perturbations before the model sees them. Ensembles spend it through redundancy, combining models with different architectures, training data, or preprocessing paths so that a perturbation that fools one member is less likely to fool all of them.

#### Evaluation and testing {#sec-robust-ai-evaluation-testing-4b54}

Evaluating adversarial defenses closes the budget loop: the system must measure which attacks the defense actually covers and what performance it sacrifices under controlled attack conditions. Robustness metrics quantify resilience through accuracy on adversarial examples, the distortion required to fool the model, and performance over attack budgets. Standardized benchmarks such as MNIST-C [@mu2019mnistc], CIFAR-10-C, and ImageNet-C [@hendrycks2019benchmarking] measure common corruptions rather than malicious worst-case behavior, so their results occupy a different cell of @tbl-robust-ai-evaluation-matrix.

Empirical attack evaluation must be adaptive to the defense\index{Adaptive Evaluation!gradient masking pitfalls}. The evaluator should know the preprocessing, detector, randomness, ensemble, and rejection rule; optimize through differentiable components; use expectation over transformation for randomness; test transfer and query-based attacks when gradients are unavailable; and include the complete pipeline rather than a saved model alone. Multiple random restarts and attack budgets can strengthen evidence within that threat model, but a passed PGD test proves neither that PGD found the inner maximum nor that semantic, physical, or differently normed attacks are covered. Only a certificate establishes a guarantee, and only for its stated input, norm, radius, and assumptions.

```{python}
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ STANDARDIZED ROBUSTNESS EVALUATION (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Paragraph after the adaptive-evaluation paragraph and
# │          @fig-robustbench-progress.
# │
# │ Goal: Show measured progress and residual cost of adversarial defenses
# │       under one standardized attack.
# │ Show: Best AutoAttack accuracy 44% (2018) -> 75% (2024) at clean ~94%;
# │       four published defenses fall to ~0% under the standardized attack.
# │ How: Year maxima and filters over Literature.Series.RobustBenchCIFAR10Linf.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Literature
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_percent

def _dated(rows):
    return [r for r in rows if r["year"] and r["unreliable"] != "True"]

def _best(rows, year):
    return max((r for r in rows if int(r["year"]) == year), key=lambda r: r["autoattack_acc"])

def _broken(rows, floor):
    return [r for r in rows if r["autoattack_acc"] < floor]

# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
class RobustBenchProgress:
    """Best robust accuracy by year and defenses broken by AutoAttack."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    rows = _dated(Literature.Series.RobustBenchCIFAR10Linf.entries)
    first_year, last_year = 2018, 2024
    broken_floor = 5.0  # percent AutoAttack accuracy; below this a defense provides no robustness

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────
    best_first = _best(rows, first_year)
    best_last = _best(rows, last_year)
    broken = _broken(rows, broken_floor)
    entry_count = len(rows)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(40 <= best_first["autoattack_acc"] <= 48 and 70 <= best_last["autoattack_acc"] <= 80, "Prose quotes ~44% (2018) and ~75% (2024).")
    check(best_last["clean_acc"] - best_last["autoattack_acc"] > 15, "Prose says a large clean-robust gap remains.")
    check(len(broken) == 4, f"Prose says four defenses fall to near zero, got {len(broken)}.")
    check(all(r["clean_acc"] > 85 for r in broken), "Prose says the broken defenses kept high clean accuracy.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    entry_count_str = fmt_int(entry_count)
    best_first_pct_str = fmt_percent(round(best_first["autoattack_acc"] / 100, 2), precision=0, style="prose")
    best_last_pct_str = fmt_percent(round(best_last["autoattack_acc"] / 100, 2), precision=0, style="prose")
    best_last_clean_pct_str = fmt_percent(round(best_last["clean_acc"] / 100, 2), precision=0, style="prose")
    best_last_fail_pct_str = fmt_percent(round(1 - best_last["autoattack_acc"] / 100, 2), precision=0, style="prose")
    broken_floor_str = fmt_percent(broken_floor / 100, precision=0, style="prose")
```

RobustBench approximates that discipline at scale with one standardized, parameter-free attack ensemble, AutoAttack, applied to every published defense under one fixed threat model, which for CIFAR-10 is a perturbation of at most 8/255 per pixel in the $\ell_\infty$ norm [@croce2021robustbench; @croce2020autoattack]. @Fig-robustbench-progress plots the `{python} RobustBenchProgress.entry_count_str` dated entries. The best accuracy under attack rose from `{python} RobustBenchProgress.best_first_pct_str` in 2018 to `{python} RobustBenchProgress.best_last_pct_str` in 2024, while the same model kept `{python} RobustBenchProgress.best_last_clean_pct_str` accuracy on clean images, so even the strongest defense still fails on about `{python} RobustBenchProgress.best_last_fail_pct_str` of attacked inputs. The four entries at the bottom of the plot are published defenses that keep high clean accuracy yet fall below `{python} RobustBenchProgress.broken_floor_str` accuracy under the standardized attack, the result an evaluation that is not adaptive to the defense can miss.

::: {#fig-robustbench-progress fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Standardized Robustness Evaluation of Published Defenses**: Clean accuracy (gray) and accuracy under AutoAttack (red) for CIFAR-10 defenses on the RobustBench leaderboard by publication year, at a perturbation budget of 8/255 in the $\ell_\infty$ norm. Filled red points trained only on CIFAR-10; hollow points used additional data. The line tracks the best robust accuracy published by each year. Points near zero are defenses that do not withstand the standardized attack. Data from @croce2021robustbench." fig-alt="Scatter plot of CIFAR-10 accuracy from 0 to 100 percent against publication years 2018 to 2024. Gray clean-accuracy points cluster between about 80 and 95 percent. Red robust-accuracy points spread lower, between about 30 and 75 percent, with a stepped line for the best so far rising from 44 percent in 2018 to about 66 percent in 2020 and 75 percent in 2024. Four red points sit near zero in 2019 and 2020."}

```{python}
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ STANDARDIZED ROBUSTNESS EVALUATION (FIGURE)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-robustbench-progress.
# │
# │ Goal: Show clean and AutoAttack accuracy by year with best-so-far line.
# │ Show: Gray clean points, red robust points (hollow = extra data), step line.
# │ How: RobustBenchProgress (above); book_style.setup_plot().
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import numpy as np
from binder.tools.figures import style as book_style

fig, ax, COLORS, plt = book_style.setup_plot(figsize=(7, 3.7))
_C = RobustBenchProgress
_rng = np.random.default_rng(0)  # horizontal jitter only, so points within one year do not overlap
_jit = {id(r): _rng.uniform(-0.18, 0.18) for r in _C.rows}
_x = lambda r: int(r["year"]) + _jit[id(r)]
ax.scatter([_x(r) for r in _C.rows], [r["clean_acc"] for r in _C.rows], s=14, color=COLORS["grid"], label="Clean accuracy", zorder=2)
_ex = [r for r in _C.rows if r["additional_data"] == "True"]
_no = [r for r in _C.rows if r["additional_data"] != "True"]
ax.scatter(
    [_x(r) for r in _no], [r["autoattack_acc"] for r in _no], s=20, color=COLORS["RedLine"], label="Under attack, CIFAR-10 data only", zorder=3
)
ax.scatter(
    [_x(r) for r in _ex],
    [r["autoattack_acc"] for r in _ex],
    s=20,
    facecolors="white",
    edgecolors=COLORS["RedLine"],
    linewidths=1.2,
    label="Under attack, additional data",
    zorder=3,
)
_years = list(range(_C.first_year, _C.last_year + 1))
_run, _bx, _by = 0.0, [], []
for _y in _years:
    _run = max(_run, max(r["autoattack_acc"] for r in _C.rows if int(r["year"]) == _y))
    _bx.append(_y - 0.5)
    _by.append(_run)
_bx.append(_years[-1] + 0.5)
_by.append(_run)
ax.step(_bx, _by, where="post", color=COLORS["RedLine"], lw=1.6, label="Best under attack so far", zorder=4)
ax.set_xticks(_years)
ax.set_xlim(_C.first_year - 0.6, _C.last_year + 0.6)
ax.set_ylim(-3, 100)
ax.set_xlabel("Publication year")
ax.set_ylabel("CIFAR-10 accuracy (%)")
ax.legend(fontsize=9, loc="lower center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 1.01), ncol=2, frameon=False)
plt.show()
plt.close()
```

:::

### Robustness of generative models {#sec-robust-ai-robustness-generative-ai-941b}

The defenses above were built for classifiers, and generative models need the same discipline in a new form. An aligned language model of the Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3) class can pass its safety evaluations and still comply with a harmful request once an automatically optimized suffix is appended to the prompt, and suffixes optimized against open models transfer to other models [@zou2023]. That suffix is an adversarial example in token space, found by gradient-guided search over discrete tokens rather than continuous pixels. Generative models also fail without any attacker. Their output is open-ended text rather than a label, so the robustness question changes from whether a label flips under perturbation to whether the generated content preserves factuality, policy constraints, and task intent across prompt variations. A fluent answer can be factually baseless while latency and uptime stay healthy, which makes hallucination\index{Hallucination!generative AI} the generative form of silent failure.

The evaluation discipline of @tbl-robust-ai-evaluation-matrix carries over with three adjustments. First, correctness needs a named reference. A hallucination rate is meaningful only against a stated evidence source, such as the retrieved context, a verified knowledge base, or an expert-labeled answer set, and it counts the generated claims that this reference does not support. The measured rate also depends on the model, the retrieval context, the prompt design, and the sampling temperature, so a reported rate holds only for its prompt set and decoding settings and cannot be carried to another domain without re-measurement. Second, the perturbation budget becomes a family of prompt variations. Paraphrases, reordered context, and inserted distractors play the role that the $\ell_\infty$ ball plays for an image classifier, and robustness is reported for each family. Third, the slices are domains and user populations, because an aggregate rate can hide a domain in which the model invents answers, just as the Google Photos failure hid inside aggregate image accuracy.

Detecting a hallucination on an individual request is the per-request competence problem of @sec-robust-ai-selective-prediction with an open-ended output. Token entropy\index{Hallucination!token entropy limitations} and log-probability can expose instability in a generation, but neither is a factuality score. A model can assign high probability to a false statement learned from its data, or low probability to a correct but rare statement. Production routing must therefore calibrate these signals against task-specific errors and combine them with evidence checks, retrieval support, or external verification.

The self-consistency\index{Self-Consistency!definition} technique samples multiple reasoning paths\index{Self-Consistency!reasoning path sampling} or answers for the same query. Disagreement supplies an instability signal that can route the request for review; agreement supplies weaker evidence because correlated samples can repeat the same misconception or unsupported claim. Sequence-level entropy has the same limitation: it can serve as a calibrated routing feature for a named task, but it does not transform uncertainty into truthfulness. The signal also has a price. Each additional sample repeats the decode phase for that request, so drawing $\SelfConsistencySampleCount$ samples multiplies its decode work roughly $\SelfConsistencySampleCount$-fold; only the prompt's prefill can be shared, when the serving system reuses the prompt's cached key-value state. Like the noise samples of randomized smoothing, this cost lands on the compute term of every request it covers, and the same remedy applies. The expensive signal should be spent on the requests whose cheap signals already indicate uncertainty rather than on all traffic. The operational contract must measure error conditional on the routing score and provision the refusal, retrieval, tool, or human path that receives flagged generations.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Reuse of a shared prompt's cached key-value state across requests is established in @sec-inference-scale-prefix-caching-8e8b.
:::

In retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)\index{Retrieval-Augmented Generation!retrieval noise} architectures, robustness depends heavily on the quality of the retrieved context. **Retrieval noise**\index{Retrieval Noise!definition}, the injection of irrelevant or conflicting documents into the prompt, can distract the model, causing it to ignore its internal parametric knowledge and propagate errors from the context. Robust RAG deployments can use re-ranking models and context verifiers to filter out noise before it reaches the generation step. Their evaluation must separate retrieval failure from generation failure. Measuring answer support separately for requests whose retrieved context contains the answer and for requests whose context does not shows whether errors come from the retriever or from a model that ignores or overrides good evidence. The retrieval corpus is also an input an attacker may be able to write to, so a planted document can corrupt retrieval evidence or carry prompt injection, and the ingress controls of @sec-robust-ai-data-poisoning-defenses-d070 apply to it. It becomes a training-poisoning path if the pipeline later admits it into learning.

Language interfaces also carry the input-level attacker into text. Prompt injection\index{Prompt Injection!robustness failure}, a failure of the boundary between control and data, embeds instructions in user content or retrieved documents so that the model overrides its system prompt. The payload can arrive through a legitimate input channel, so permission to submit content does not make that content trustworthy. External access controls still constrain which data or tools the surrounding system exposes. From the robustness side, evaluation asks whether the content induces behavior outside the intended output contract, and it is measured the way adversarial robustness is measured: as an attack success rate over an injection suite matched to the threat model, run by an evaluator who knows the system prompt and filters. Keeping those details secret is not a defense, because optimized suffixes transfer across models.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Prompt injection as a failure of the boundary between control and data is established in @sec-security-privacy-llmspecific-threat-vectors-65f2.
:::

A common deployment pattern adds **output guardrails**\index{Output Guardrail!definition}, lightweight classifiers that scan generated text for policy violations\index{Output Guardrail!policy enforcement} or toxicity before the response returns to the user. A guardrail threshold trades the same two quantities as a selective-prediction threshold. Each false positive refuses or escalates a legitimate response, so the false-positive rate multiplied by the legitimate-request rate estimates false refusals or escalations; each false negative is residual risk that reaches the user. Total diverted load also includes correctly flagged harmful responses. The arrival rate at each refusal, retrieval, or human path is the incoming request rate multiplied by the fraction routed to that path under the policy, counting both true and false flags. Choosing the threshold from a curve measured on representative traffic, rather than from the classifier's default, allows the team to compare that load with the path's capacity. The guardrail also adds a model inference to every response, so its latency counts against the serving deadline. Finally, a guardrail is itself a model with its own decision boundary, so it carries the same obligation as any other defense and must pass the adaptive evaluation above against an attacker who knows it is there.

Adversarial training, certified defenses, and generative guardrails address attacks on model inputs at inference time within bounded threat models. They do not establish that the model was trained on trustworthy data. If an adversary compromises the data pipeline long before the model is compiled, inference-time behavioral tests may reveal a backdoor, but cannot by themselves establish the integrity of the training pipeline. The data poisoning attacks described earlier demand their own class of defenses.

::: {#chk-robust-ai-defense-budget .callout-checkpoint title="Choosing and budgeting an adversarial defense"}

An adversarial defense is a budgeted response to a specific threat model. Stronger guarantees commonly change clean accuracy, compute, latency, or coverage, but the direction and magnitude depend on the workload, model, defense, and evaluation boundary.

**Matching defense to threat**

- [ ] **Worst-case evaluation**: explain why passing a white-box PGD test provides empirical evidence only for the evaluated model, norm, budget, restarts, and attack implementation rather than a general worst-case guarantee.
- [ ] **Threat-model fit**: match the defense emphasis to an API-facing classifier and a safety-critical road-sign detector, and explain why adversarial training alone does not transfer between them.

**Reasoning about the budget**

- [ ] **Certified vs. empirical**: explain when randomized smoothing's sampling cost favors asynchronous auditing or a selective serving path rather than assuming that every certified deployment has the same latency constraint.
- [ ] **Defense budget**: compare input detection with intrinsic model robustness for a low-risk component using measured clean accuracy, robust accuracy, compute, latency, and coverage rather than assuming a fixed clean-accuracy tax.

:::

## Data Poisoning Defenses {#sec-robust-ai-data-poisoning-defenses-d070}

A recommendation model may retain its overall accuracy while promoting an attacker's chosen item to a small group of users. Defending against that failure requires testing the targeted behavior as well as securing the integrity of the training supply chain. Source permissions set the security boundary, and robustness evaluation measures what happens when poisoned records or updates cross it anyway. The defense therefore runs as four ordered layers along the data path:

1. **Ingress controls** establish provenance and access limits, dictating which sources may contribute or modify data.
2. **Anomaly detection and sanitization** inspect candidate records before training and filter suspicious submissions.
3. **Robust training objectives** reduce the weight that extreme residuals receive for poisoned samples that evade ingestion filtering, although they do not by themselves bound parameter updates.
4. **Representation learning** reduces the model's reliance on brittle features that poisoned instances can exploit.

Each layer covers a distinct point along the data path, and no single detector can substitute for end-to-end controls. While representation learning broadens defense to handle ordinary distribution shift, it cannot prove that the training corpus is uncompromised.

For the recommendation system, the interception layer in @fig-adversarial-attack-injection examines contributed ratings before they reach training. Its decisions must preserve provenance so later model failures can be traced back to the accepted records.

::: {#fig-adversarial-attack-injection fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Data Poisoning and Interception Workflow**: Adversaries inject malicious rows into a user-item rating matrix to manipulate model behavior. A defense layer analyzes contributed data and removes suspected malicious records before training. This can reduce poisoning risk but does not guarantee an uncorrupted model." fig-alt="A rating matrix with four user rows and two red sybil rows that rate item 3 as 1 and item 4 as 5. A gray bracket spans every row of the matrix, and a single line leaves its midpoint and forks. The upper branch, a dashed red arrow labeled no filter, reaches a red compromised model box in which item 3 is buried and item 4 boosted. The lower branch, a gray arrow, enters a green interception box labeled spectral scores, influence audit. Inside it, six scored rows drawn as small cell strips split: four plain rows pass to a kept stack, and the two red rows are diverted into a dashed red quarantine tray. A green arrow labeled filtered carries the kept rows to a candidate model box marked validate before release."}
![](images/svg/poisoning-interception.svg)
:::

### Ingress and anomaly controls {#sec-robust-ai-anomaly-detection-techniques-bc27}

Poisoning defense begins at the data boundary, before any statistical detector runs. The pipeline must know which sources are allowed to contribute training data, how their authenticity is verified, and which roles can modify accepted records. Strong governance enforces the principle of least privilege,[^fn-least-privilege-ml] logs data access and modification events, and gives each accepted batch a source identity. These controls do not prove that every record is clean, but they bound the attack surface and give anomaly findings a traceable origin.

[^fn-least-privilege-ml]: **Principle of Least Privilege**\index{Principle of Least Privilege!definition}\index{Least Privilege!ML pipeline security}: Articulated by @saltzer1975, this principle restricts access rights to the minimum necessary for each component. In an ML pipeline, a training job allowed to read unverified sources has an additional path through which adversarial data can enter, so write and read rights become part of the poisoning attack surface. The same principle governs the model registry\index{Model Registry!least-privilege access control}, the artifact store that maps version identifiers to weight files and controls which alias (for example, `staging`, `production`) resolves to which checkpoint. Promotion to the `production` alias should be restricted to a narrow, audited set of automated evaluation services and named release engineers; if a researcher's credentials are compromised, excluding those credentials from promotion authority blocks that direct path to replacing the live model, while other authorized paths still require scrutiny.

After the source boundary, anomaly detection asks whether a candidate training example belongs to the distribution that the pipeline intended to learn from. The cheapest tests compare each record against the bulk distribution: Z-score filtering, Tukey's method, and Mahalanobis distance flag examples whose feature values sit far from normal ranges. These tests are useful because they are fast enough to run at ingestion, but they catch only poisons that look like statistical outliers in raw feature space. For high-dimensional or multimodal data, raw-feature distances are a weak signal: a manipulated image or caption that passes raw-feature checks may separate from clean examples in a pretrained vision or language model's embedding space. That separation depends on the encoder and attack, so it must be measured rather than inferred from the use of a learned representation. Applying Mahalanobis distance\index{Mahalanobis Distance!latent representation filtering} or clustering to those representations tests a different hypothesis from raw-feature screening. The pipeline must check whether the resulting outliers correspond to malicious contributions or to legitimate variation it needs to retain.

More coordinated attacks require structure-aware checks. Clustering methods such as K-means, DBSCAN, and hierarchical clustering look for anomalous groups or isolated points rather than single extreme values. The autoencoder ingestion gate diagrammed in @fig-autoencoder adds a learned representation to the screening pipeline: the model compresses inputs through a bottleneck layer $\EncoderLatentRepresentation$, accepting records whose reconstruction error $\AutoencoderReconstructionError$ falls below threshold $\ResponseThreshold$ and quarantining anomalous outliers. Each method has a failure mode. Clean-label poisons need not be statistical outliers. Clustering depends on the representation, and autoencoders can reconstruct unfamiliar inputs well or learn an attack pattern from a contaminated reference corpus. Each gate therefore needs evaluation on both poisons and legitimate rare examples.

::: {#fig-autoencoder fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Autoencoder Ingestion Gate**: An autoencoder trained on trusted data learns to compress inputs through a narrow latent layer $\EncoderLatentRepresentation$ and reconstruct them. Reconstruction error supplies an anomaly score, not proof that an input is poisoned. The gate accepts records whose reconstruction error $\AutoencoderReconstructionError$ stays at or below a threshold $\ResponseThreshold$ calibrated on held-out clean data and quarantines the rest." fig-alt="Symmetric hourglass network: an encoder narrows seven input units through five and three hidden units to a two-unit latent layer, and a decoder expands back to seven reconstructed outputs. An arrow from the output leads to a reconstruction error panel, L rec equals the squared norm of x minus x hat, containing a horizontal score axis labeled L rec at its arrow end and split by a dashed threshold tau. Left of tau is a green accept zone, L rec at most tau, holding a stacked cluster of green record dots at low scores; right of tau is a red quarantine zone, L rec greater than tau, holding two red record dots at high scores."}
![](images/svg/autoencoder.svg)
:::

#### Sanitization and preprocessing {#sec-robust-ai-sanitization-preprocessing-f883}

Sanitization turns anomaly signals into training-set changes before the poison reaches optimization. A suspicious record can be rejected, quarantined for review, down-weighted during training, or kept with an explicit provenance flag. Routine cleaning still matters: deduplication, missing-value handling, type checks, range constraints, and cross-field validation remove many low-effort poisoning attempts while improving ordinary data quality.

Data provenance\index{Data Provenance!ML pipelines} and lineage tracking make those decisions reversible. Each datum needs a record of its source, transformations, validation outcomes, and movement through the pipeline. When a model later exhibits a poisoning symptom, lineage lets the operator trace\index{Data Lineage!poisoning rollback} model dependencies back to candidate source batches, investigate which contributions caused the behavior, estimate which trained models consumed confirmed compromised examples, and decide whether to remove, relabel, or reweight the affected records.

When suspicious data has already entered the corpus, sanitization moves from source checks to representation checks. Spectral signatures\index{Spectral Signature!data sanitization} exploit separation between clean and poisoned samples in a learned representation [@tran2018spectral]. In the backdoor attacks studied by Tran and colleagues, the trigger created a strong signal in the target class's activations. Projecting centered representations onto the top singular vector\index{Spectral Signature!singular value decomposition} and removing high-scoring samples exposed many poisoned records without requiring prior knowledge of the trigger. The method depends on sufficient separation relative to within-group variation; an effective backdoor does not by itself guarantee a usable spectral signature. Filtering therefore requires attack-specific evaluation and checks for discarded clean samples.

Influence functions\index{Influence Functions!data sanitization} [@koh2017understanding] serve a narrower debugging role. They approximate how infinitesimally increasing a training point $\TrainingExample$'s weight changes the model's loss for a test point $\TestExample$, without retraining. The fitted parameters are the trained model's weights, and the Hessian is the curvature matrix of the average training loss at those parameters. Its inverse translates a small change in a training point's weight into an approximate change in the fitted parameters.
